content_units: Best Fit for a Gluten-Free Solo Cook on an $80/Week Budget
For your priorities,   App B   is the strongest paid choice, and   App C free/basic   is the best no-risk starting point.
If you want the easiest day-to-day planning with solid gluten-free support and a worthwhile upgrade,   App B gives the best value per year  .
Subscription Comparison Table
App   Price   Gluten-Free Support   Ease of Use   Best For   Upgrade Value
App A     USD 12/month       Strong  : allergy filters     Very easy  : auto grocery list   Simple weekly planning   Fair

App B     USD 79/year       Moderate to strong  : likely workable via recipe/nutrition organization, but no explicit allergy filter listed     Easy  : meal prep mode helps batch cooking   Solo cooks who want planning + nutrition     Best overall

App C     Free   basic /   USD 5/month   premium     Limited on free  , better on premium with planner/macros     Basic  : manual list slows things down   Budget-first testing   Good only if you’ll use premium features
Option 1:   App B     Best balance of recipe depth, nutrition visibility, and long-term value     About USD 6.58/month effective cost
Option 2:   App A     Easiest gluten-free filtering from the start, but weaker for nutrition-aware budgeting     Best pure convenience pick
Option 3:   App C Premium     Cheapest paid tier, but still less convenient than A or B for shopping and filtering     Best low-cost upgrade
What Matters Most for Your Situation
Ease of use
-   App A wins   on simplicity because the   auto grocery list   removes the most annoying weekly task.
-   App B   is close behind because   meal prep mode   is very helpful when cooking for one person and stretching ingredients across several meals.
-   App C basic   is weakest because a   manual shopping list   adds friction every week.
Gluten-free diet filtering
-   App A is the safest match   because it explicitly includes   allergy filters  .
-   App B   may still work well, but based on the details given, it does   not explicitly confirm allergy filtering  .
-   App C   looks weakest for strict filtering unless the premium planner meaningfully improves organization.
Paid upgrade justification
-   App B’s paid plan is justified   if you want one app to handle planning well for the whole year.
- 500 recipes gives more variety, which helps avoid repetition when cooking for one.
- Nutrition breakdown helps compare meals against your budget and personal health goals.
- Meal prep mode is especially useful for single-person cooking because it reduces waste.
-   App A’s paid plan is justified   only if your biggest pain point is   finding safe gluten-free recipes quickly   and generating a grocery list fast.
-   App C premium   is justified only if you want the   cheapest upgrade   and can tolerate a more limited recipe library and weaker convenience.
Practical Recommendation for an $80/Week Grocery Budget
Recommended pick: App B
Why it fits best:
- Annual price is reasonable relative to the features.
- Better recipe variety helps you rotate affordable staples without getting bored.
- Nutrition breakdown can help you choose meals that are filling and cost-efficient.
- Meal prep mode supports batch cooking, which is one of the easiest ways to stay within   USD 80/week  .
Best alternative: App A
Choose this instead if:
- You need   confident gluten-free filtering   more than nutrition data.
- You want the fastest weekly workflow with the least setup.
Lowest-risk path: App C free, then premium only if you like the workflow
Choose this if:
- You want to test whether you’ll actually use a meal-planning app before paying.
- You are okay with ads and some manual effort at first.
Decision Context
I’m assuming:
- “Allergy filters” in App A include a reliable gluten-free filter.
- App B supports meal selection well but does   not   explicitly guarantee allergen filtering beyond what was stated.
- Your   USD 80/week grocery budget   is for food shopping, not app cost, so app pricing is judged mainly on convenience and value.

Choose App B
Start Free with C
